metadata.title: Guard Retention Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master guard retention in BJJ. Complete guide covering frame creation, hip mobility, and recovery. Defensive position with 60% retention success at advanced level.

overview: Guard Retention Bottom is the defensive framework employed when your guard is under attack and you're working to prevent the pass. This position represents the critical transition phase between established guard and potential guard pass, requiring constant movement, proper framing, and intelligent space management. Unlike static guard positions, guard retention is highly dynamic, involving continuous hip escapes, frame resets, and defensive reactions to maintain guard structure. The position demands excellent conditioning, timing, and positional awareness as you navigate the opponent's passing attempts while seeking opportunities to re-establish full guard or counter-attack. Success in guard retention separates competent guard players from elite ones, as it determines whether you maintain bottom position advantage or concede top control. The ability to retain guard under pressure is fundamental to modern BJJ, particularly in competition where persistent guard passers will test your defensive capabilities repeatedly throughout a match.
state_invariants: Bottom player's hips remain mobile and off the mat, maintaining dynamic positioning to prevent opponent from settling into passing position with weight and pressure
Active frames established between bottom player's limbs and opponent's body, creating distance and preventing chest-to-chest contact that signals guard pass completion
Bottom player's shoulders remain on or near the mat while hips face opponent, maintaining guard structure orientation despite pressure and preventing back exposure
At least one connection point (hook, grip, frame) maintained between bottom and top player to enable guard recovery, even if traditional guard structure is compromised
Bottom player's spine aligned and core engaged to enable shrimping movements, with knees pulled toward chest to maintain defensive ball position under pressure
prerequisites: Opponent has initiated guard passing sequence from established guard position
Bottom player's guard structure is under direct attack with at least one guard component compromised
Space has been created between bottom player and opponent, requiring active frames or hooks to prevent pass completion
Bottom player maintains some degree of hip mobility despite opponent's passing pressure
Opponent has not yet achieved chest-to-chest contact or established three points of control indicating completed pass
key_principles: Maintain constant hip mobility through shrimping and inversion to prevent opponent from pinning hips to mat
Create and reset frames continuously using hands, forearms, shins, and feet to manage distance
Keep at least one connection point (hook, grip, frame) to opponent at all times to enable guard recovery
Generate space through explosive hip movements before opponent can consolidate passing position
Recover full guard by using frames to create distance, then reestablishing hooks and control points
Never allow opponent to achieve chest-to-chest contact without active defensive response
Use timing and opponent's momentum against them to create counter-opportunities during passing attempts

common_errors.error: Allowing hips to remain flat on mat during guard retention attempts
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily settles weight and completes pass without resistance
common_errors.correction: Continuously shrimp and elevate hips off mat, maintaining dynamic positioning to prevent opponent from pinning hips down

common_errors.error: Posting hands on mat instead of creating active frames on opponent's body
common_errors.consequence: Loss of distance management allows opponent to close space and achieve chest-to-chest contact
common_errors.correction: Keep hands on opponent's hips, shoulders, or biceps to create frames that actively manage distance and prevent forward pressure

common_errors.error: Committing fully to single guard recovery attempt without backup plan
common_errors.consequence: Opponent anticipates and counters specific recovery, completing pass when initial attempt fails
common_errors.correction: Chain multiple guard recovery options together, using opponent's reactions to first attempt to set up second and third options

common_errors.error: Excessive grip fighting that prevents hip movement and mobility
common_errors.consequence: Static positioning allows opponent to consolidate passing position while bottom player focuses on grips
common_errors.correction: Prioritize hip mobility and movement over grip battles during guard retention, using frames more than grips initially

common_errors.error: Turning away from opponent or exposing back during retention attempts
common_errors.consequence: Opponent transitions to back control or takes dominant position from back exposure
common_errors.correction: Always keep chest facing opponent during guard retention, using granby rolls and inversions that maintain front-facing orientation

common_errors.error: Giving up on guard retention too early and accepting inferior position
common_errors.consequence: Unnecessary concession of guard position when recovery was still possible
common_errors.correction: Fight until opponent achieves three points of control (chest-to-chest plus two points), maintaining active retention until pass is truly completed

common_errors.error: Neglecting to use legs and feet as frames during retention sequences
common_errors.consequence: Limited framing options reduce effectiveness of distance management
common_errors.correction: Employ feet on hips, shin shields, and knee frames as primary distance management tools before opponent gets close enough to require hand frames

expert_insights.danaher: Guard retention is fundamentally about creating a hierarchical system of defensive frames that force the opponent to solve multiple problems sequentially rather than simultaneously. The biomechanical principle is to create distance through frames positioned at optimal leverage points - feet on hips being the first line of defense, followed by shin shields, then knee frames, and finally hand frames as a last resort. Each frame buys time for hip escape movements that reset the defensive sequence. The key systematic error I observe is students treating guard retention as isolated reactions rather than as a connected defensive system where each frame transitions logically to the next based on opponent pressure. Your hips must remain in constant motion, creating angles that make it geometrically impossible for the opponent to achieve the chest-to-chest alignment required for pass completion. Master this defensive hierarchy and your guard becomes exceptionally difficult to pass.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In high-level competition, guard retention separates champions from everyone else because elite passers will test your guard relentlessly. My approach emphasizes offensive defense - I'm not just preventing the pass, I'm actively hunting for sweep and submission opportunities during retention sequences. When my guard is under attack, I'm thinking three moves ahead: if this frame fails and I shrimp here, I can shoot for deep half; if they counter that, I can invert to reverse De La Riva. The physical demand is enormous, which is why conditioning is critical - your retention must remain sharp into the championship rounds when fatigue sets in. Against world-class passers like Felipe Pena or Keenan Cornelius, you can't rely on single defensive reactions; you need chains of defensive options that flow together seamlessly. The mental aspect is equally important - never give up on guard retention until your shoulders are pinned and they have clear chest-to-chest control with three points of contact.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Traditional guard retention often gets too defensive and reactive, which is why 10th Planet methodology emphasizes offensive defense from retention positions. When your guard is under attack, that's actually a prime opportunity to enter into our system because the opponent is committed to their passing sequence and potentially vulnerable to counters. We use the lockdown, rubber guard entries, and deep half transitions as guard retention tools, not just as established positions. The key is staying dangerous even when you're defending - make them respect your offense so they can't just bulldoze through your guard. I teach students to think of guard retention as a scramble opportunity rather than a purely defensive phase. Create chaos, maintain movement, and look for unconventional angles that disrupt their passing rhythm. Your retention should feel exhausting for them, not just for you. Also, don't be afraid to go inverted, use rolling attacks, or transition to turtle if it means maintaining offensive options - giving up traditional guard structure temporarily is acceptable if you're setting up your offense.

metadata.title: Guard Retention | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master guard retention in BJJ. Essential defensive concepts for maintaining guard position against passing attempts. Learn frames, hip escapes, and recovery strategies.

overview:
Guard Retention represents the fundamental defensive skill set required to maintain guard position when facing an opponent's passing attempts. Rather than a single static position, guard retention is a dynamic defensive state characterized by constant adjustment, framing, and hip movement to prevent the opponent from establishing control past the legs. This skill forms the foundation of bottom game survival and is essential for all practitioners regardless of experience level.

Effective guard retention relies on understanding spatial relationships, maintaining distance through frames and leg positioning, and utilizing hip mobility to recover guard structure when compromised. The position demands continuous assessment of threats and appropriate responses, often requiring rapid transitions between different guard configurations to prevent the pass. Modern guard retention integrates concepts from multiple guard types, allowing practitioners to flow between positions rather than stubbornly defending a single guard structure.

Mastery of guard retention fundamentally changes a practitioner's bottom game, transforming defensive scrambles into opportunities for re-establishment and counter-attacks. The best guard players are not those who never get passed, but those who can continuously recover and re-establish guard even under sustained pressure.
state_invariants: At least one leg maintains barrier function between practitioner's hips and opponent's hips, creating defensive space through knee shield, butterfly hook, spider guard grip, or other leg-based frame that prevents opponent from settling their weight

Hips remain mobile with ability to shrimp, bridge, or rotate away from pressure, maintaining connection to mat through shoulders and upper back while lower body stays dynamic and responsive to passing threats

Hands actively manage distance through frames on opponent's hips, shoulders, or head, or maintain grips on sleeves, collars, or pants that control opponent's posture and prevent them from achieving dominant grips or angles

Practitioner's spine maintains structural integrity with active core engagement, avoiding flattened position where shoulders and hips are simultaneously pinned to mat, instead keeping at least one dimension of movement available
prerequisites: Opponent attempting to pass guard from standing or kneeling position
Practitioner on bottom with legs between themselves and opponent
Active defensive awareness of passing threats and pressure direction
Sufficient hip mobility to perform shrimping and bridging movements
Understanding of basic framing concepts and distance management
key_principles: Maintain at least one leg as active barrier between your hips and opponent's hips at all times
Keep hips mobile and ready to shrimp away from pressure, never allowing opponent to flatten both shoulders and hips simultaneously
Use frames (hands on hips, biceps, or head) to create and maintain distance when legs are compromised
Continuously adjust guard type based on opponent's passing angle rather than defending single configuration
Anticipate passing direction and begin recovery movements before opponent achieves dominant position
Prioritize space creation over submission attempts when guard structure is threatened
Chain multiple retention techniques together, using failed defenses as setups for subsequent recoveries

common_errors.error: Allowing both shoulders and hips to flatten against mat simultaneously
common_errors.consequence: Complete loss of mobility and inability to generate shrimping or bridging movements, leading to inevitable pass
common_errors.correction: Always keep at least one dimension of movement available by maintaining shoulder connection while hips are mobile, or vice versa

common_errors.error: Gripping too tight without moving hips, relying purely on grip strength to prevent pass
common_errors.consequence: Opponent breaks grips through superior leverage or simply waits until arms fatigue, then passes easily
common_errors.correction: Use grips to control opponent's posture and create opportunities for hip movement, not as primary defense mechanism

common_errors.error: Attempting to defend single guard configuration stubbornly rather than adapting
common_errors.consequence: Opponent exploits weaknesses of that specific guard structure and passes through well-prepared path
common_errors.correction: Flow between guard types based on opponent's passing direction, treating guard as fluid defensive system

common_errors.error: Waiting until guard is completely broken before attempting recovery
common_errors.consequence: Opponent achieves sufficient control that recovery becomes exponentially more difficult or impossible
common_errors.correction: Begin recovery movements at first sign of guard structure being threatened, using anticipation rather than reaction

common_errors.error: Crossing ankles or locking feet when not in appropriate position
common_errors.consequence: Limited hip mobility and vulnerability to ankle locks or foot locks, plus reduced ability to adjust quickly
common_errors.correction: Keep legs independent and mobile unless specifically in position that requires foot lock (closed guard, body triangle, etc.)

common_errors.error: Framing with arms fully extended and locked, creating static barrier
common_errors.consequence: Opponent simply redirects around rigid frames or collapses them with superior weight and pressure
common_errors.correction: Maintain bent arm frames with active extension, allowing dynamic adjustment as opponent changes angle

common_errors.error: Looking away from opponent or closing eyes during retention scrambles
common_errors.consequence: Loss of visual information about opponent's weight distribution and passing direction, leading to mistimed defenses
common_errors.correction: Maintain visual contact with opponent's hips and shoulders to read passing intentions and time escapes properly

expert_insights.danaher: Guard retention is not merely a defensive skill but represents the fundamental control of distance and angle that defines modern guard play. The primary mechanical principle underlying effective retention is the maintenance of what I call 'defensive barriers' - structural elements (legs, frames, grips) that prevent the opponent from achieving the critical distance where their weight can be applied to your torso. Most students make the error of treating guard retention as a reactive scramble when in fact it should be a proactive system of spatial control. Your legs should function as mobile barriers that continuously adjust based on your opponent's angle of attack, never allowing a direct path to side control. The hips must remain the most mobile part of your body, capable of instant direction changes through shrimping and bridging movements. When teaching guard retention, I emphasize the concept of 'creating problems faster than your opponent can solve them' - each defensive movement should force your opponent to solve a new puzzle before they can consolidate position. This transforms guard retention from a series of desperate escapes into a systematic defensive framework that actually increases in effectiveness as your opponent applies more pressure.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, guard retention is what separates world champions from everyone else. I've passed the guards of multiple black belt world champions, and without exception, the hardest guys to pass are those who never let you settle into your passing rhythm. The key is being comfortable being uncomfortable - you have to embrace those scramble positions where your guard is partially broken and most people panic. That's where I actually do my best work, because I'm not trying to maintain perfect technique, I'm just solving the problem right in front of me. When someone's driving a knee cut through, I'm not thinking 'oh no my guard is broken' - I'm thinking 'cool, now I can trap that knee and enter deep half' or 'perfect, now I can granby and take the back.' The specific techniques matter less than your ability to stay calm and keep creating frames and movement when things get chaotic. My guard retention got exponentially better when I stopped trying to have perfect guard structure and started focusing on just making sure my opponent never achieves stable hip control. Even if they get past my legs temporarily, if I can keep my hips mobile and create frames, I can usually recover. The other thing that's absolutely critical in no-gi especially is grip fighting during the retention phase - if I can break their grips while they're passing, they have to reset and that gives me the time I need to recover position.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Guard retention is where the rubber meets the road in 10th Planet's whole philosophy about being comfortable in chaos. Most traditional BJJ teaches you to have this perfect guard structure and then defend it like a fortress, but that's just not realistic against a skilled passer who knows what they're doing. Instead, we focus on what I call 'flow retention' - constantly moving between different guard configurations based on where the opponent is applying pressure. If they're pressuring my right leg, I might switch to reverse De La Riva on the left. If they counter that, boom, I'm inverting or hitting a granby. The key is that you're never married to one guard type, you're just using whatever tools are available in that moment. We also spend a ton of time on the 'almost passed' positions that most schools ignore - like when you've still got one butterfly hook in but they've got an underhook and they're driving toward side control. That's not the end, that's just a different phase of retention that requires different tools. The lockdown system came from this philosophy - create a retention mechanism that's so different from traditional guards that most passers don't have prepared responses. But beyond specific techniques, the real innovation is mental - teaching students that guard retention is actually FUN, it's a puzzle to solve, not a desperate scramble. Once you internalize that mindset shift, your retention improves dramatically because you're not panicking, you're problem-solving.

metadata.title: Guard Retention Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master guard retention top position in BJJ. Learn passing strategies, pressure applications, and techniques to overcome guard retention. Complete guide for top position.

overview:
Guard Retention Top represents the top player's position when facing an opponent actively employing guard retention techniques. This is fundamentally a guard passing position where the top player must overcome defensive frames, hip movement, and leg positioning designed to prevent the pass. The position requires strategic pressure application, grip control, and systematic passing sequences to advance to more dominant positions like side control, mount, or back control.

The top player in this position must balance forward pressure with mobility, maintaining connection while preventing the bottom player from creating space or re-establishing guard. Success depends on recognizing guard retention patterns, countering defensive movements, and applying the appropriate passing strategy based on the bottom player's defensive posture. This position represents a critical battleground in modern BJJ where guard retention has become increasingly sophisticated.

Mastery of guard retention top involves understanding multiple passing systems including pressure passing, speed passing, and long-step approaches, while being able to read and counter the bottom player's defensive responses in real-time.
state_invariants: Top player maintains standing, kneeling, or headquarters posture over bottom player who is on their back or seated with clear postural control and active weight distribution through the hips and legs
Bottom player's legs are positioned between the two players, acting as barriers with active hip movement and framing to prevent passing, creating dynamic distance and defensive structures

Top player controls at least one grip on the bottom player's body, legs, or gi while working to establish passing grips, maintaining connection points to limit defensive mobility and create passing opportunities

Bottom player maintains active movement with hips facing the top player, using leg positioning and frames to create distance and prevent connection, employing defensive hip escapes and guard recovery movements

Top player's weight is strategically distributed to apply pressure while maintaining balance and mobility to follow bottom player's movements, using forward pressure to limit space creation while staying mobile enough to counter defensive repositioning
prerequisites: Bottom player has established guard position with legs between both players
Bottom player is actively using frames, grips, and hip movement to prevent the pass
Top player has broken or is working to break the initial guard structure
Top player has established standing, kneeling, or headquarters base position
Space exists between the players due to bottom player's defensive frames and movement
key_principles: Maintain constant forward pressure to limit bottom player's ability to create space and re-guard
Control bottom player's hips through grips, body position, or pressure to limit their mobility
Use grip fighting to establish dominant grips while breaking bottom player's defensive grips
Match bottom player's movements by staying centered and mobile, preventing them from getting to their side
Apply systematic passing sequences rather than random attempts, creating predictable reactions to exploit
Recognize guard retention patterns and apply appropriate counters for each defensive movement
Balance pressure with mobility to maintain connection while following defensive movement

common_errors.error: Remaining static in base without applying forward pressure or movement
common_errors.consequence: Allows bottom player to establish stronger frames, recover full guard, or create enough space to re-guard safely
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant pressure and movement to keep bottom player reactive and prevent them from establishing comfortable defensive positions

common_errors.error: Applying excessive pressure without controlling the hips first
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can use the pressure against you to hip escape, creating angles and space to recover guard
common_errors.correction: Establish hip control through grips or positioning before applying heavy pressure to prevent bottom player from using your weight to escape

common_errors.error: Focusing only on one passing direction without adapting to defensive movement
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player learns the pattern and can time their defensive responses, making passes predictable and easier to counter
common_errors.correction: Use multiple passing directions and strategies, forcing bottom player to defend different threats and creating openings

common_errors.error: Ignoring bottom player's grips on your legs, pants, or sleeves
common_errors.consequence: Strong defensive grips allow bottom player to control distance, prevent connection, and create barriers to passing
common_errors.correction: Address defensive grips immediately through grip breaks, hand fighting, or positional adjustments that nullify their effectiveness

common_errors.error: Standing too upright when bottom player has active leg positioning
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for bottom player to establish hooks, sweeps, or recover guard structure with distance management
common_errors.correction: Maintain lower posture with forward pressure while standing, using headquarters position to limit bottom player's leg mobility

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass without establishing passing grips or connections first
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player easily pushes away or creates distance since there are no meaningful connections to control their movement
common_errors.correction: Establish strong passing grips on pants, belt, or collar before initiating passing movement to maintain connection throughout

common_errors.error: Chasing bottom player's legs instead of controlling their hips and torso
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can continuously re-guard by moving their hips and legs faster than you can address each individual leg position
common_errors.correction: Focus on controlling the center of mass (hips and torso) which limits all leg movement options simultaneously

expert_insights.danaher: Guard retention top is fundamentally about creating and exploiting structural weaknesses in the bottom player's defensive posture. The bottom player's guard retention depends on maintaining critical distances and angles through frames, grips, and hip mobility. Your primary objective is to systematically remove these defensive tools through superior gripping, pressure application, and directional control. Understanding that every guard retention pattern has inherent vulnerabilities based on biomechanical limitations is crucial. When the bottom player extends to create distance, they sacrifice inside control. When they maintain tight frames, they limit their own mobility. Your passing strategy must identify which defensive choice they make and exploit the corresponding weakness. The most sophisticated passers don't simply execute techniques; they create scenarios where any defensive response opens a passing opportunity.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, guard retention top is where matches are won or lost, especially at the highest levels where everyone has excellent retention skills. My approach focuses on constant pressure and making the bottom player carry my weight while defending multiple passing threats simultaneously. I'm never static - I'm always moving their legs, changing grips, and forcing them to react. The key is understanding that modern guard retention is based on specific movement patterns and defensive sequences that athletes drill thousands of times. Your job is to disrupt those patterns by attacking from angles they don't expect or combining passes in sequences that don't follow their prepared defenses. I also use my passing to drain their energy - making them work hard to defend while I stay efficient. By the third or fourth passing attempt, they're tired and make mistakes. That's when you capitalize and finish the pass.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Guard retention top is where you need to think like a chess player, always two moves ahead. Traditional passing focuses on technique execution, but I teach my guys to create situations where the bottom player thinks they're successfully defending when they're actually moving into worse positions. Use their guard retention movements against them - if they hip escape left, be ready to attack the space they created on the right. If they frame and extend, that's when you can smash or go low. The 10th Planet approach emphasizes unconventional grips and angles that aren't part of standard retention training. We'll use twister side control entries, truck positions, or calf slicer threats from passing positions because most people don't train those defenses. You've got to be creative and unpredictable. Don't just pass their guard - make them question whether their retention techniques even work against your style.
